---
title: "Small, Typical, Large? Correlations in Published Matrices and Item Responses"
description: |
  The effect-size benchmarks people cite for individual-differences research
  come from correlations coded one at a time out of meta-analyses. IRW can come
  at the question from two other directions: whole correlation matrices as
  authors published them, and item-by-item matrices computed from raw responses.
  Both say that a typical correlation is larger than the benchmarks suggest.
  This is a pilot.
date: today
bibliography: typical_correlation_data/references.bib
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 2
---

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
irw_blue  <- "#2166ac"
irw_red   <- "#d73027"
irw_amber <- "#b8791f"
irw_grey  <- "grey50"

cache_path   <- "typical_correlation_data/typical_correlation_results.rds"
rel_path     <- "typical_correlation_data/rel_ceiling.rds"
matched_path <- "typical_correlation_data/matched_rses.rds"
cache_ok <- file.exists(cache_path) && file.exists(rel_path) && file.exists(matched_path)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = cache_ok)

f2  <- function(x) sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2))
pct <- function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")
num <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
`%||%` <- function(a, b) if (is.null(a)) b else a
# link a table name to its landing page
tl  <- function(t) sprintf("[`%s`](https://itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/%s/)", t, t)
```

```{r}
#| label: cache-warning
#| eval: true
#| output: asis
if (!cache_ok) {
  cat("::: {.callout-warning}\n## Results cache not found\n\n",
      "Run `vignettes/typical_correlation_compute.R`, `typical_correlation_rel.R` and ",
      "`typical_correlation_matched.R` from the repository root to generate it.\n:::\n", sep = "")
```

```{r}
#| label: load

.c <- readRDS(cache_path)
date_run <- .c$date_run

# ---- published side ----
cov_meta <- .c$cov_meta
pub_all  <- .c$pub_cells |> filter(!is.na(r))
pub      <- pub_all |> filter(!overlap_dropped)
pub$matrix <- paste(pub$table, ifelse(is.na(pub$group), "", pub$group))

n_pub_tables_all <- n_distinct(pub_all$table)
n_pub_tables     <- n_distinct(pub$table)
n_pub_matrices   <- n_distinct(pub$matrix)
n_pub_cells      <- nrow(pub)

pub_table <- pub |>
  group_by(table) |>
  summarise(med_abs = median(abs(r)), med = median(r), share_neg = mean(r < 0),
            n_cells = n(), n_med = median(n, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
pub_matrix <- pub |>
  group_by(table, matrix) |>
  summarise(med_abs = median(abs(r)), n_med = median(n, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# cell-level quantiles with each table weighted equally (1 / cells in table)
wq <- function(x, w, p) {
  o <- order(x); x <- x[o]; w <- cumsum(w[o]) / sum(w)
  vapply(p, function(pp) x[which(w >= pp)[1]], numeric(1))
}
pub$w_table <- 1 / ave(rep(1, nrow(pub)), pub$table, FUN = sum)
q_pub_tab  <- wq(abs(pub$r), pub$w_table, c(.25, .5, .75))
q_pub_cell <- quantile(abs(pub$r), c(.25, .5, .75))
q_pub_n    <- wq(abs(pub$r), ifelse(is.na(pub$n), 0, pub$n) * pub$w_table * n_distinct(pub$table), c(.25, .5, .75))
q_pub_mat  <- wq(abs(pub$r), 1 / ave(rep(1, nrow(pub)), pub$matrix, FUN = sum), c(.25, .5, .75))
q_pub_sgn  <- wq(pub$r, pub$w_table, c(.25, .5, .75))

# ---- subject tags (published) ----
split_tags <- function(x) lapply(strsplit(ifelse(is.na(x), "", x), "\\s*[|;,]\\s*"), function(v) v[nzchar(v)])
tag_pub <- cov_meta |>
  filter(table %in% pub_table$table) |>
  select(table, construct_type) |>
  mutate(tag = split_tags(construct_type)) |>
  unnest(tag) |>
  distinct(table, tag)

# ---- core side ----
core_cells <- .c$core_cells |> filter(!is.na(r))
core_meta  <- .c$core_meta
core_info  <- .c$core_info
core_fail  <- .c$core_fail
core_meta$gap <- core_meta$mean_abs_item_rest_r - core_meta$mean_item_rest_r
low_gap <- core_meta$table[!is.na(core_meta$gap) & core_meta$gap < 0.005]

core_table <- core_cells |>
  group_by(table) |>
  summarise(med_abs = median(abs(r)), med = median(r), share_neg = mean(r < 0),
            med_abs_pearson = median(abs(r_pearson), na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(core_info, by = "table") |>
  mutate(low_gap = table %in% low_gap)
core_cells$w_table <- 1 / ave(rep(1, nrow(core_cells)), core_cells$table, FUN = sum)
q_core_tab  <- wq(abs(core_cells$r), core_cells$w_table, c(.25, .5, .75))
q_core_pear <- with(core_cells[!is.na(core_cells$r_pearson), ],
                    wq(abs(r_pearson), w_table, c(.25, .5, .75)))
lg <- core_cells[core_cells$table %in% low_gap, ]
q_core_lg_sgn <- wq(lg$r, lg$w_table, c(.25, .5, .75))
q_core_lg_abs <- wq(abs(lg$r), lg$w_table, c(.25, .5, .75))

core_tags <- .c$core_tags
tag_core <- if (!is.null(core_tags)) {
  core_tags |>
    filter(table %in% core_table$table) |>
    select(table, construct_type) |>
    mutate(tag = split_tags(construct_type)) |>
    unnest(tag) |>
    distinct(table, tag)
} else tibble(table = character(), tag = character())

# ---- reliability ceiling ----
rel <- readRDS(rel_path)$cells |> filter(!is.na(r), !is.na(ceiling))
# ---- matched RSES ----
mt <- readRDS(matched_path)
```

```{r}
#| label: derived
# ---- overlap and counts ----
n_dropped_tables <- n_pub_tables_all - n_pub_tables
n_core_ok <- nrow(core_table)
meth <- table(core_info$method)
nm <- function(k) if (k %in% names(meth)) meth[[k]] else 0L

# ---- published, by construct type ----
tp  <- pub_table |> inner_join(tag_pub, by = "table")
lev <- tp |> group_by(tag) |> summarise(m = median(med_abs), k = n(), .groups = "drop") |> arrange(m)
lev_k <- lev |> filter(k >= 10)
hi <- lev_k |> slice_max(m, n = 1); lo <- lev_k |> slice_min(m, n = 1)

# ---- published, by framework ----
fw <- cov_meta |>
  filter(table %in% pub_table$table) |>
  distinct(table, framework) |>
  mutate(fw = split_tags(framework)) |>
  unnest(fw, keep_empty = TRUE) |>
  mutate(grp = case_when(
    fw %in% c("TPB", "TAM", "UTAUT", "RAA", "HAPA", "HBM", "SCCT") ~ "behaviour or technology-acceptance model",
    fw == "status_attainment" ~ "status attainment",
    TRUE ~ "no framework tag")) |>
  distinct(table, grp) |>
  left_join(pub_table, by = "table")
fw_sum <- fw |> group_by(grp) |>
  summarise(tables = n(), median = median(med_abs), q25 = quantile(med_abs, .25),
            q75 = quantile(med_abs, .75), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(median))
fwb <- fw_sum |> filter(grp == "behaviour or technology-acceptance model")
fwn <- fw_sum |> filter(grp == "no framework tag")

# ---- core, by construct type and keying ----
tc_tab <- core_table |> inner_join(tag_core, by = "table")
levc <- tc_tab |> group_by(tag) |> summarise(m = median(med_abs), k = n(), .groups = "drop") |> arrange(m)
km <- tag_core |> mutate(low_gap = table %in% low_gap) |> group_by(tag) |>
  summarise(k = n(), flagged = sum(!low_gap), share_flagged = mean(!low_gap), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(k >= 10) |> arrange(desc(share_flagged))
neg_lg   <- mean(lg$r < 0)
neg_rest <- mean(core_cells$r[!core_cells$table %in% low_gap] < 0)

# ---- toy aggregation example ----
k_toy   <- 10
rbar    <- q_core_tab[2]
rel_toy <- k_toy * rbar / (1 + (k_toy - 1) * rbar)
true_r  <- q_pub_tab[2] / rel_toy

# ---- matched RSES ----
pm <- mt$pub
ov_groups <- mt$pub_meta$group[!is.na(mt$pub_meta$overlaps) & mt$pub_meta$overlaps != ""]
pm_ind <- pm[!pm$group %in% ov_groups, ]
m_pub_all <- median(pm$value); m_pub_ind <- median(pm_ind$value)
m_core_poly <- median(abs(mt$core$value)); m_core_pear <- median(abs(mt$core$r_pearson))

# ---- reliability ceiling ----
n_rel_tab <- n_distinct(rel$table)
ex <- rel |> filter(exceeds)
ex_tab <- ex |> count(table, sort = TRUE)

# ---- widget payload: table-weighted ECDF of |r| on a grid, by side and tag ----
grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)
ecdf_w <- function(x, w) vapply(grid, function(g) sum(w[x <= g + 1e-9]) / sum(w), numeric(1))
ecdf_side <- function(cells, tags, side, min_tables = 5) {
  out <- list(tibble(side = side, tag = "All construct types", x = grid,
                     F = ecdf_w(abs(cells$r), cells$w_table), k = n_distinct(cells$table)))
  for (t in sort(unique(tags$tag))) {
    tb <- tags$table[tags$tag == t]
    if (length(tb) < min_tables) next
    cc <- cells[cells$table %in% tb, ]
    out[[length(out) + 1]] <- tibble(side = side, tag = t, x = grid,
                                     F = ecdf_w(abs(cc$r), cc$w_table), k = length(tb))
  }
  bind_rows(out)
}
tc_ecdf <- bind_rows(
  ecdf_side(pub, tag_pub, "published matrices"),
  ecdf_side(core_cells, tag_core, "core, between items")
) |> mutate(F = round(F, 4))
ojs_define(tc_ecdf = tc_ecdf, tc_blue = irw_blue, tc_amber = irw_amber)
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
This vignette (the analysis design, the compute scripts and the writing below) was produced largely by Claude (Anthropic), working from a task specification and with human review. It is a pilot: the published side uses every matrix in `irw_cov` (`r n_pub_tables_all` tables), but the core side uses a seeded random sample of `r .c$n_core_sampled` of the `r num(.c$n_eligible)` eligible core tables, each capped at `r num(.c$max_people)` randomly chosen people and `r .c$max_items` randomly chosen items. Numbers will move when the core pass is run on everything. The design is under discussion in [datapages/irw#451](https://github.com/datapages/irw/issues/451); comments there are welcome. Check the compute scripts directly if you are relying on the numbers here.
:::

## Where does your correlation fall?

Pick a correlation and, if you like, a construct type. The widget reports where that value sits among the correlations in published matrices and among the correlations between items in core tables, with each table counted once.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
tc = transpose(tc_ecdf)
tc_tags = ["All construct types", ...Array.from(new Set(tc.map(d => d.tag))).filter(t => t !== "All construct types").sort()]
viewof tc_r = Inputs.range([0, 1], {step: 0.01, value: 0.30, label: "Your correlation, |r|"})
viewof tc_tag = Inputs.select(tc_tags, {label: "Construct type"})
tc_fmt = v => v.toFixed(2).replace(/^0/, "")
tc_at = side => {
  const d = tc.find(e => e.side === side && e.tag === tc_tag && Math.abs(e.x - tc_r) < 0.005);
  return d ? d : null;
}
tc_line = side => {
  const d = tc_at(side);
  if (!d) return `Too few ${side === "published matrices" ? "published" : "core"} tables are tagged *${tc_tag}* to say (fewer than five).`;
  const what = side === "published matrices" ? "correlations in published matrices" : "correlations between items in core tables";
  return `It is larger than **${Math.round(100 * d.F)}%** of the ${what} (${d.k} tables).`;
}
tc_gs = tc_r >= 0.30 ? "relatively large" : tc_r >= 0.20 ? "typical" : tc_r >= 0.10 ? "small" : "smaller than small"
md`An |r| of **${tc_fmt(tc_r)}**:

- ${tc_line("published matrices")}
- ${tc_line("core, between items")}
- Gignac and Szodorai's guidelines would call it **${tc_gs}**.`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  height: 260,
  marginLeft: 50,
  x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "|r|"},
  y: {domain: [0, 1], label: "share of correlations at or below", tickFormat: "%"},
  color: {domain: ["published matrices", "core, between items"], range: [tc_blue, tc_amber], legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([0.10, 0.20, 0.30], {stroke: "#999", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.line(tc.filter(d => d.tag === tc_tag), {x: "x", y: "F", stroke: "side", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleX([tc_r], {stroke: "#333", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
    Plot.dot(tc.filter(d => d.tag === tc_tag && Math.abs(d.x - tc_r) < 0.005), {x: "x", y: "F", fill: "side", r: 5})
  ]
})
```

The dashed lines are Gignac and Szodorai's guidelines (.10, .20, .30).

## The short answer

A typical correlation is larger than the benchmarks suggest, and how much larger depends on what is being correlated. Between the scales that authors print in published matrices, the median |r| is **`r f2(q_pub_tab[2])`**. Between items within one instrument, it is **`r f2(q_core_tab[2])`** (`r f2(q_core_pear[2])` if we stick with Pearson). Both sit well above the .19 that is usually quoted as "typical" for individual-differences research. The rest of the page explains where these numbers come from and why the two differ.

## Where the benchmarks come from

The benchmarks most often cited are those of @gignac2016. From 708 correlations drawn out of meta-analyses, the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles were .11, .19 and .29, and they suggested reading .10, .20 and .30 as small, typical and relatively large. @bosco2015 did the same for applied psychology using 147,328 coded correlations from metaBUS and found a median |r| of .16.

Both are built from correlations that someone coded one at a time. IRW holds two other kinds of evidence:

- **Published matrices** (`irw_cov`). These are whole correlation and covariance matrices as authors printed them. Most are correlations *between scales*, chosen because the authors had a model they wanted to fit.
- **Core response data.** Any core table can be turned into an item-by-item correlation matrix with `irw_fetch(<table>, source = "cov")`. These are correlations *between items within one instrument*, computed the same way for every table. Nobody chose which cells to print.

These answer somewhat different questions, and we think the gap between them is as informative as either number on its own.

## Published matrices

Some published tables share a sample, so we keep one table from each such group; this drops `r n_dropped_tables` tables, using the `overlaps` record field. That leaves `r n_pub_tables` tables, `r num(n_pub_matrices)` matrices and `r num(n_pub_cells)` off-diagonal cells. Covariances are converted to correlations. Each table counts once: its cells share a single unit of weight. This keeps the large meta-analytic tables, some of which hold dozens of matrices, from swamping everything else.

With that weighting, the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of |r| are **`r f2(q_pub_tab[1])`, `r f2(q_pub_tab[2])` and `r f2(q_pub_tab[3])`**. Each is roughly double the corresponding Gignac and Szodorai percentile (.11, .19, .29).

```{r}
#| label: fig-pub-dist
#| fig-cap: "Median |r| per published table. Dashed lines: Gignac and Szodorai's 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles."
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(pub_table, aes(med_abs)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.025, boundary = 0, fill = irw_blue, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(.11, .19, .29), linetype = "dashed", colour = irw_red) +
  labs(x = "median |r| within the table", y = "tables")
```

Does the weighting drive this? Not especially:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pub-weights
tibble(
  weighting = c("each table equally (headline)", "each matrix equally", "each cell equally",
                "each table equally, then by sample size", "each table equally, signed r"),
  p25 = c(q_pub_tab[1], q_pub_mat[1], q_pub_cell[1], q_pub_n[1], q_pub_sgn[1]),
  p50 = c(q_pub_tab[2], q_pub_mat[2], q_pub_cell[2], q_pub_n[2], q_pub_sgn[2]),
  p75 = c(q_pub_tab[3], q_pub_mat[3], q_pub_cell[3], q_pub_n[3], q_pub_sgn[3])
) |>
  mutate(across(p25:p75, f2)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Weighting", "25th", "50th", "75th"), align = "lrrr")
```

The last row keeps signs. Between-scale signs depend on how each scale was scored, so the signed distribution is only a rough guide; `r pct(mean(pub$r < 0))` of published cells are negative.

### By subject

The cov subject tags give each matrix a construct type. A table carrying more than one tag counts in each.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pub-tags
#| fig-cap: "Median |r| per published table, by construct-type tag. The number of tables is on the right."
#| fig-height: 4.5
tp$tag <- factor(tp$tag, levels = lev$tag)
ggplot(tp, aes(med_abs, tag)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, alpha = 0.35, size = 1, colour = irw_blue) +
  geom_text(data = lev, aes(x = 1.02, y = tag, label = k), hjust = 0, size = 3.3, colour = irw_grey) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1.08)) +
  labs(x = "median |r| within the table", y = NULL)
```

Among tags with at least 10 tables, **`r hi$tag`** matrices run hottest (median `r f2(hi$m)`) and **`r lo$tag`** matrices coolest (median `r f2(lo$m)`). The proposal predicted that matrices fitted to attitude and behaviour models (TPB, UTAUT, TAM) would run hotter than personality or attainment ones. Construct type is too coarse to test that. The `framework` tag is the better test, but so far it is set on only a few tables:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-framework
fw_sum |> mutate(across(median:q75, f2)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Framework", "Tables", "Median of table medians", "25th", "75th"), align = "lrrrr")
```

The `r fwb$tables` tables fitted to a behaviour or technology-acceptance model (TPB, TAM, UTAUT, RAA, HAPA, HBM, SCCT) have a median |r| of `r f2(fwb$median)`, against `r f2(fwn$median)` for untagged tables. That is in the predicted direction, but `r fwb$tables` tables is too few to lean on.

## Item-level matrices from core

The core pass computed an item-by-item matrix for `r n_core_ok` of the `r .c$n_core_sampled` sampled tables (`r nrow(core_fail)` failed; see the end of the page). Binary items get tetrachoric correlations (`r nm("tetrachoric")` tables), items with 3 to 8 categories get polychoric (`r nm("polychoric") + nm("polychoric (correct = 0)")`), and anything else gets Pearson (`r nm("pearson")`). Two details of the estimation are worth noting:

- Before estimation, each item's codes are recoded to consecutive integers, keeping their order. psych counts categories from the range of the codes, so an item scored 0/5/10/15 otherwise trips its eight-category limit.
- For `r nm("polychoric (correct = 0)")` sparse tables, psych's continuity correction for empty cells fails, and those tables are estimated without it (`correct = 0`).

Pearson is also computed on the raw codes for every table, as a check.

Response direction is not harmonised across core items. A reverse-keyed item stored raw correlates negatively with the rest of its scale, and that sign means nothing substantively, so the headline uses |r|. Weighting each table equally, the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of inter-item |r| are **`r f2(q_core_tab[1])`, `r f2(q_core_tab[2])` and `r f2(q_core_tab[3])`**. With Pearson throughout they are `r f2(q_core_pear[1])`, `r f2(q_core_pear[2])` and `r f2(q_core_pear[3])`. The choice of estimator alone moves the median by `r f2(q_core_tab[2] - q_core_pear[2])`.

### Keying: |r| and a known-direction subset

Could the |r| headline be hiding something? The core metadata carries each table's mean item-rest correlation twice, signed (`mean_item_rest_r`) and absolute (`mean_abs_item_rest_r`). If no item correlates negatively with the rest of its scale, the two agree. Tables where they agree to within .005 (`r sum(core_table$low_gap)` of the `r n_core_ok` here) show no sign of reverse keying, so we can read their signed r directly. Only `r pct(neg_lg)` of item pairs in this subset are negative, against `r pct(neg_rest)` in the rest. This is a proxy, not a keying record: an instrument whose subscales correlate negatively can open the gap without any reverse keying.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-keying
tibble(
  set = c("all sampled tables, |r|", "low-gap subset, |r|", "low-gap subset, signed r"),
  tables = c(n_core_ok, sum(core_table$low_gap), sum(core_table$low_gap)),
  p25 = c(q_core_tab[1], q_core_lg_abs[1], q_core_lg_sgn[1]),
  p50 = c(q_core_tab[2], q_core_lg_abs[2], q_core_lg_sgn[2]),
  p75 = c(q_core_tab[3], q_core_lg_abs[3], q_core_lg_sgn[3])
) |>
  mutate(across(p25:p75, f2)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Set", "Tables", "25th", "50th", "75th"), align = "lrrrr")
```

Restricting to the low-gap subset raises the median from `r f2(q_core_tab[2])` to `r f2(q_core_lg_abs[2])`, and within the subset signed and absolute r agree at these percentiles. The subset is not a random slice of core, though. It changes the mix of construct types:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-keying-mix
tag_core |>
  mutate(low_gap = table %in% low_gap) |>
  count(tag, low_gap) |>
  group_by(low_gap) |> mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |> ungroup() |>
  select(-n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = low_gap, values_from = share, values_fill = 0) |>
  rename(flagged = `FALSE`, `low gap` = `TRUE`) |>
  arrange(desc(`low gap`)) |>
  mutate(across(-tag, pct)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Construct type", "Among tables showing reverse keying", "Among low-gap tables"),
        align = "lrr")
```

Among construct types with at least 10 sampled tables, **`r km$tag[1]`** tables are flagged most often (`r km$flagged[1]` of `r km$k[1]`) and **`r km$tag[nrow(km)]`** tables least often (`r km$flagged[nrow(km)]` of `r km$k[nrow(km)]`). Going in, we expected the subset to tilt towards binary achievement tests. In this sample it does not: cognitive/educational tables are a small share of both groups. The shift is instead away from personality scales and towards opinion/attitude scales.

### By subject

```{r}
#| label: fig-core-tags
#| fig-cap: "Median inter-item |r| per core table, by construct-type tag. The number of tables is on the right."
#| fig-height: 4.5
tc_tab$tag <- factor(tc_tab$tag, levels = levc$tag)
ggplot(tc_tab, aes(med_abs, tag)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, alpha = 0.45, size = 1.2, colour = irw_amber) +
  geom_text(data = levc, aes(x = 1.02, y = tag, label = k), hjust = 0, size = 3.3, colour = irw_grey) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1.08)) +
  labs(x = "median inter-item |r| within the table", y = NULL)
```

## Items versus scales

```{r}
#| label: fig-both
#| fig-cap: "Median |r| per table: published matrices (mostly between scales) and core item-level matrices (within one instrument). Each table counts once. Dashed lines: Gignac and Szodorai's percentiles."
#| fig-height: 4
both <- bind_rows(
  pub_table |> transmute(side = "published matrices", med_abs),
  core_table |> transmute(side = "core, between items", med_abs)
)
ggplot(both, aes(med_abs, colour = side, fill = side)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.2, adjust = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(.11, .19, .29), linetype = "dashed", colour = irw_grey) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(irw_amber, irw_blue)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(irw_amber, irw_blue)) +
  labs(x = "median |r| within the table", y = "density", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Why are item pairs hotter than scale pairs? Two forces pull in opposite directions. Averaging items into a scale score raises reliability, and higher reliability raises the observed correlation between two scales. But items within one instrument are written to measure the same thing, while two scales in a published matrix usually measure different things.

A simple case shows which force wins. Take a `r k_toy`-item scale whose items correlate at the core median, `r f2(rbar)`. By the Spearman-Brown formula its reliability is `r k_toy` × `r f2(rbar)` / (1 + `r k_toy - 1` × `r f2(rbar)`) = `r f2(rel_toy)`. Two such scales that correlate at the published median, `r f2(q_pub_tab[2])`, would have true scores correlating at about `r f2(q_pub_tab[2])` / `r f2(rel_toy)` = `r f2(true_r)`. Aggregation therefore works in favour of the scale pairs, not against them. Even with perfect reliability, two typical published scales would correlate at about `r f2(true_r)`, still below the `r f2(rbar)` that items within one instrument manage. The gap is about content: the scales in a published matrix mostly measure different constructs, while the items within an instrument measure one.

### One instrument on both sides: the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale

So far the two sides differ in both what is correlated and who was sampled. What happens when we hold the instrument fixed? The Rosenberg scale is the one instrument confirmed on both sides at the item level. `r tl("gnambs_2018_rses10")` holds `r n_distinct(pm$group)` published 10-item matrices from the meta-analysis by @gnambs2018, and `r tl("rosenberg_selfesteem")` holds raw responses, of which we use `r num(mt$n_core_people)` randomly chosen respondents.

- **Published:** the median item-pair r across the `r n_distinct(pm$group)` matrices is `r f2(m_pub_all)`. Leaving out the `r length(ov_groups)` matrices whose `overlaps` field says they share data with `rosenberg_selfesteem`, it is `r f2(m_pub_ind)`. The published matrices are recoded so that all items point the same way: only `r pct(mean(pm$value < 0))` of cells are negative.
- **Core:** `r pct(mean(mt$core$value < 0))` of item pairs are negative, which reflects the scale's five reverse-keyed items stored raw. The median |r| is `r f2(m_core_pear)` with Pearson and `r f2(m_core_poly)` with polychoric correlations.

Even with the instrument held fixed, the core sample correlates more strongly than the published samples. The estimator accounts for part of the gap; the rest is a difference between samples. Some of the meta-analysis's matrices were reconstructed from published loadings, which the table's notes record.

## A reliability ceiling check

Two scales with reliabilities $\rho_i$ and $\rho_j$ can correlate at most $\sqrt{\rho_i \rho_j}$, which is the observed correlation when their true scores correlate perfectly. `r n_rel_tab` published tables report reliabilities (`rel` rows), covering `r num(nrow(rel))` scale pairs. Of these, **`r nrow(ex)` (`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * nrow(ex) / nrow(rel))`) exceed the ceiling**, spread over `r nrow(ex_tab)` tables. The median overshoot is `r f2(median(abs(ex$r) - ex$ceiling))`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rel
ex |>
  group_by(table) |>
  summarise(pairs = n(), max_over = max(abs(r) - ceiling), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(pairs)) |>
  mutate(table = tl(table), max_over = f2(max_over)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Table", "Pairs above the ceiling", "Largest overshoot"))
```

A pair above the ceiling is not necessarily an error. Coefficient alpha understates reliability when items are not tau-equivalent, the reliabilities may come from a different sample than the correlations, and correlations between latent variables are not bounded this way. Mostly, the check flags tables that merit a second look at the source.

## Caveats

- **Published matrices are curated.** Authors print the variables they modelled, and IRW's holdings lean on CC BY articles and open deposits. The published side answers "typical in openly licensed published matrices", not "typical in psychology".
- **Core has its own selection.** It holds whatever data people chose to share, and the pilot excludes longitudinal, sparse (density below .5) and very large tables.
- **|r| is biased upward near zero.** Taking absolute values folds noise around zero into positive values, which inflates small correlations. This matters little for inter-item pairs, which mostly sit well above zero, but it is why both sides are summarised with |r| for the comparison.
- **The estimators differ.** Published matrices are mostly Pearson on scale scores, while the core side uses polychoric and tetrachoric correlations, which run higher than Pearson on the same items (see the Pearson figures above).
- **Within- and between-construct pairs are mixed** on the published side. Separating them needs construct labels on variables, which IRW does not have yet.

## What the full run would add

- The core pass on every eligible table, not just `r .c$n_core_sampled`, with breakdowns by sample and framework tags as well as construct type.
- Fuller `framework` tagging on the published side, so the behaviour-model comparison rests on more than a handful of tables.
- More instruments matched across the two sides, beyond the Rosenberg scale.

```{r}

  cat("\n**Core tables that failed in this run:**\n\n")
  cat(paste0("- ", tl(core_fail$table), ": ", core_fail$error, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
}
```
